questions.q: What was an *iqta* during the Delhi Sultanate, and who was its head?
questions.a: An *iqta* was a territorial revenue assignment, and its holder was called a *muqti* or *iqtadar*. If a student thinks an *iqta* was a permanent hereditary kingdom, they are confusing the Sultanate administrative assignment with later Mughal *jagirs* or independent regional kingdoms, missing that *muqtis* were frequently transferred by the Sultan to prevent them from becoming too powerful.

questions.q: Why did Sultans like Ala-ud-din Khalji implement strict market control and fixed prices for goods in Delhi?
questions.a: Ala-ud-din Khalji fixed prices and controlled markets so he could maintain a large standing army on a limited treasury without having to increase soldiers' cash salaries. A wrong answer—such as thinking he did it out of kindness for poor citizens—reveals a failure to understand that medieval economic administration was primarily driven by military survival and imperial defense needs.

questions.q: If a newly appointed *muqti* in a distant province refused to send tax revenue to Delhi, how would the central Sultanate administration respond based on historical precedent?
questions.a: The Sultan would dispatch royal inspection officers (*barids* or spies) to investigate, and if rebellion occurred, send imperial royal troops to suppress the revolt, replace the *muqti*, or transfer him to a smaller territory. A student who believes the Sultan would simply ignore the provincial governor fails to understand the centralized nature of the Delhi Sultanate and the strict accountability demanded by rulers like Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

questions.q: How did the administrative reforms of Ala-ud-din Khalji differ from those of Muhammad bin Tughlaq regarding agricultural taxation?
questions.a: Ala-ud-din Khalji increased land revenue to 50 percent of the produce collected directly in grain to feed Delhi, whereas Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted innovative monetary experiments (token currency) and raised taxes in the Doab region during a famine, leading to agrarian crisis. A wrong answer suggests the student views all Sultanate rulers as having identical economic policies, missing how individual rulers adapted administration to crises.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The administrative system of the Delhi Sultanate was purely foreign and had no roots in Indian traditions." Defend your position with historical evidence.
questions.a: This statement is false because while Turkic rulers introduced Islamic legal frameworks and military titles, they largely retained existing local administrative structures, village headmen (*muqaddams*), and local revenue officials (*patwaris*). A student who agrees with the statement ignores historical continuity, failing to recognize that governing a massive agrarian population required using established Indian revenue collection machinery.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical administrative blueprint for a 14th-century Sultan who wants to prevent provincial governors from rebelling while keeping the treasury full. What three checks would you put in place?
questions.a: A strong answer must include: (1) regular transfer of *muqtis* every few years, (2) independent royal accountants and intelligence agents (*barids*) stationed in provinces to audit taxes, and (3) separate collection of land revenue from military command duties. A poor answer focuses only on harsh punishments without structural checks and balances.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ systems under the Delhi Sultanate refer to the centralized political structures, revenue collection methods (such as *iqta* system), and military governance established by Turkic and Afghan rulers in India between the 13th and 16th centuries.

Fill in the blank: Imagine visiting a massive medieval fort like Qutb Minar or Tughlaqabad in Delhi and wondering how an emperor sitting in the capital managed distant ______ like Bengal or the Deccan without telephones or cars.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can explain how the *iqta* system functioned as an administrative tool for revenue collection and military mobilization, and can compare Delhi Sultanate governance methods with earlier Mauryan or Gupta administrative models.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine visiting a massive medieval fort like Qutb Minar or ______ in Delhi and wondering how an emperor sitting in the capital managed distant provinces like Bengal or the Deccan without telephones or cars.
